title: 3-Read Friday #19: Reflection, Worksheets, and Christmas Maths
author: Craig Barton
summary: Craig Barton's 3-Read Friday #19 curates three posts on professional reflection, task design, and seasonal resources. Jo Castelino contrasts a novice and an experienced teacher running the same explanation-and-questioning routine to argue that experience is really reflection in disguise, and that discussing the specific decisions behind a lesson with a more experienced colleague can accelerate that reflection. Dylan Kane defends the humble worksheet, describing one he built using Variation Theory that changed the classroom atmosphere by giving discouraged students an accessible, confidence-building on-ramp. Colleen Young rounds up her annually updated maths Advent calendar and Christmas-themed resources for the run-up to December. Barton frames the set as a mix of the reflective and the practical -- how teachers get better, how one specific resource can shift a lesson's energy, and a seasonal resource for the weeks ahead.
points: Jo Castelino's contrast between Mr K and Ms Y shows that simply copying an experienced teacher's routine is not enough; discussing the specific in-the-moment decisions behind it is what actually transfers expertise.

Dylan Kane's Variation Theory worksheet -- changing as little as possible from one problem to the next -- visibly changed his students' engagement compared to a more cognitively demanding curriculum activity earlier in the same lesson.
Kane's broader point: worksheets are neither inherently progressive nor traditionalist; what matters is the thinking the specific problems require, not the paper they're printed on.
Barton's pairing of a reflection-on-practice post with a seasonal resource roundup shows the newsletter's dual register: professional growth and week-to-week classroom logistics.
quotes: This is a powerful post about the challenges novice teachers face when observing their more experienced colleagues.
The best part is that Jo gives us a series of questions that teachers of all experiences can ask when they watch their colleagues in action in order to understand the reasons behind their decisions.

He describes why he chose to use a particular worksheet in the vain of the intelligent practice activities on my variation theory website, and contrasts this with two more challenging questions he asked his students later in the lesson.
The point about a worksheet making students (and possibly teachers) feel safe really resonated.

Colleen has done a great job of compiling the very best Christmas-themed maths resources and advent calenders out there to ensure you can inject some festive fun into your lessons whilst also keeping your students thinking hard about maths.
